title: ITER: why, where and who
description: Why seven rival Members build one fusion machine together, how the site at Cadarache was chosen, how the work is shared, and how ITER's schedule changed from 2016 to 2024.

sources.title: ITER Organization: ITER Members (seven Members, cost shares, in-kind contributions, Domestic Agencies, results and IP shared, UK, Switzerland, cooperation partners)
sources.note: EU 45.6 %, the six others 9.1 % each; about nine-tenths in kind; Members share 100 % of the results and the intellectual property; Switzerland a member of Fusion for Energy from 1 January 2026.

sources.title: ITER Organization: 28 June 2005, a home at last (the site contest)
sources.note: Candidates Clarington (withdrawn December 2003), Vandellòs, Cadarache, Rokkasho; EU choice of Cadarache 26 November 2003; deadlock in December 2003; decision in Moscow on 28 June 2005; the Broader Approach as compensation; about 75 km north of Marseille.

sources.title: ITER Organization: ITER France (host-country obligations)
sources.note: 180-hectare site, 42-hectare platform; requirements met; international school in Manosque (opened 2007); ITER Itinerary.

sources.title: ITER Organization: Facts and figures
sources.note: 104 km itinerary from a Mediterranean port; about 5,000 people on site and in offices (2026).

sources.title: ITER baseline press conference summary, 3 July 2024 (PDF)
sources.note: 2016 baseline: first plasma 2025, full plasma current 2033, D–T 2035. 2024 baseline: research operation 2034, D–D 2035, full magnetic energy 2036, D–T 2039. Reasons: COVID-19, first-of-a-kind components, quality problems, optimistic schedules.

sources.title: ITER Organization: Component repair (vacuum vessel bevels, thermal shield cracking), September 2023
ITER press release: two-thirds of the tokamak core in place, 29 July 2026 (PDF)
sources.note: Sixth of nine sector modules in the pit on 28 July 2026, almost six months ahead of schedule; the last one planned for mid-2027.
